text: Good day, everyone. My name is Fathani Ramwaja from the South
African National Biodiversity Institute.
I will be talking about our efforts to build a sustainable and robust
geodiversity data ecosystem. The South African National
Biodiversity Institute has implemented standardized data
management strategies for South Africa's national
botanical and zoological collections.
The project focuses on transitioning legacy data
into
FAIR, which is Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and
Reusable data sets using globally recognized
informatics standards.
Central to this architecture is the National Biodiversity
Information System, which
integrates data from diverse institutional
partners using standardized software platforms such as
BRMS 8 for botanical records and Specify for
zoological data.
A primary challenge in
national data integration is metadata harmonization,
particularly regarding taxonomic inconsistencies.
To resolve this, SANBI employs the TaxonMatch
algorithm, a fuzzy logic implementation
that matches misspelled or varying species names to
an authoritative taxonomic backbone.
This ensures that data retrieved from the central repository
remains high quality and interoperable regardless of
the contributor's internal interpretations.
SANBI distributes authoritative dictionaries,
including taxa with offers, and
gazetteer data to ensure quality at the point of capture.
The controlled data flow
is designed for scalability and data integrity.
Institutions push new or change data to
staging instances where automated data quality checks are
applied before the records move to the production environment.
This process is supported by extract, transform, load
packages that synchronize data at regular intervals.
The system supports complex geographic data ecosystems
by allowing users to perform spatial searches, such
as drawing
polygons on maps to retrieve species coordinates.
SANBI utilizes the digital extended specimen in
NBIS via persistent identifiers linked
across various repositories. The specimen extends
to species description data, locality information,
collections data, literature and references, common names, and
uses data, as well as images and other media,
which is all highlighted on the NBIS system.
By providing the infrastructure and common standards, SANBI
enables a scalable, unified web portal that
promotes data cleaning, reduces duplication, and harnesses
collective knowledge for environmental monitoring and research.
This system needs to be sustainable,
and SANBI practices a diversified funding model.
SANBI is mandated under the National Environmental
Management Biodiversity Act, which we call NEMBA, to
manage information regarding South Africa's biodiversity as follows.
We must collect, generate, process,
coordinate, and disseminate information about biodiversity and the
sustainable use of indigenous
biological resources and establish and maintain national
databases in this regard.
So having an official mandate facilitates a minimum
flow of fiscal funds, which is under the infrastructure
grant.
However, we are also leveraging external project
grants for functional extensions.
We are also investigating establishing a dedicated
biodiversity information fund to receive, hold, and
transparently disburse non-governmental,
international, and donor funds without financial
year-end clawbacks.
So we need to align the National Biodiversity Information System
with our national priorities. That is explicitly
linking SANBI's information platforms to the National
Biodiversity Economy Strategy, the National
Development Plan, and climate change adaptation priorities,
demonstrating how biodiversity data supports green economy
investment, streamlines EIAs, which is
environmental impact assessments, and reduces regulatory delays.
We need to establish a biodiversity data core
investment consortium that is partnering with
universities, science councils, and South
African national parks to share data hosting, collection,
and maintenance costs while SANBI provides national
coordination, standards, and visibility.
BaDi, which is a project,
provides an example of collaborative platform development
for African wetland and waterbird data.
We need to establish a multisectoral information steering committee,
bringing together government, academia,
NGOs, which is non-government organizations, and the
private sector
to strengthen platform governance,
unlock core funding, share licensing costs,
and leverage in-kind technical expertise.
We need to develop value-added analytics and advisory
services
Keep core biodiversity data openly accessible in line
with the member act,
while offering paid services such as customized data
analysis, spatial modeling, screening
reports, and decision support tools to commercial
users.
We need to adopt a modular cloud-based
architecture and monitoring and
evaluation framework
to maintain scalable
modular systems while avoiding unnecessary administrative
growth and track usage, policy uptake,
environmental impact applications, and decision-making impacts
to demonstrate return on investment and strengthen
treasury and grant funding cases.
Our proposed sustainability roadmap starts
to secure the core funding, which is protect baseline public
funding and statutory functions, then align
with national
priorities,
to link NB's outcomes to biodiversity economy and
NDP, National Development Plan, climate and
environmental impact assessment priorities.
Core investment, create consortium and steering mechanisms for
shared costs and expertise. Diversify,
establish donor fund mechanisms and targeted value-added
services.
Demonstrate value, measure use, policy uptake,
regulatory impact, and return on investment.
And preserve capability, invest in people,
succession, archiving, and resilient infrastructure.
Thank you for the opportunity for presenting this talk.
